"You're certain he didn't follow you?" Commander Croft asked, his eyes scanning the narrow confines of the control room. "The man from the docks?"

"Positive, sir," Jack Riley, the young American radioman, answered. "Finch and I made sure of it. We circled the block twice. He was just a fisherman looking for a handout."

"A fisherman who knew your names," the commander stated flatly, turning his gaze on the British sonar technician. "What's your assessment, Finch?"

"He was clumsy, sir," the English youth replied, his voice soft but clear. "Too clumsy for a professional. But Jack's right. We lost him clean before we reached the rendezvous."

"Good," Commander Croft said, though the grim set of his mouth did not relax. "Because if he had followed you, this entire submarine and its crew would now be at the bottom of the bay."

Riley blinked. "Sir? For a simple drop? I thought we were just delivering a new type of sonar jammer to the Resistance."

"You were," the commander said, and he ran a hand over the cold steel of the periscope housing. "But you must understand something, Riley. In this war, nothing is ever simple. You believed your mission was to deliver that canister. It was, but not for the reason you thought."

He paused, and the only sound was the low hum of the electric motors and the gentle creak of the hull under the immense pressure of the deep.

"Those jammers, sir," Finch spoke up. "The frequency they operate on is highly unusual. I've never seen anything like it. It wouldn't fool a German destroyer's hydrophone for more than a minute."

"It isn't supposed to," Croft said, a flicker of approval in his eyes. "That frequency isn't for a destroyer's hydrophone. It's for a specific listening post located in Hamburg. A listening post run by the Abwehr's top cryptographers."

"You mean," Riley gasped, the color draining from his face, "you wanted them to find it?"

"I mean I'm counting on them finding it!" the commander confirmed sharply. "That 'jammer' is a broadcaster. Once activated, it sends out a repeating, coded message. The Abwehr will pick it up. They'll think they've captured a new Allied device. They'll spend weeks trying to crack the code, and when they do, they'll believe they've hit the jackpot."

The horrible, brilliant truth of the plan began to dawn on Jack Riley. It was a bluff, but a bluff of such magnitude it made his head spin.

"What's in the message, sir?" he asked, his voice barely a whisper.

"The complete convoy schedule for Operation Anvil," Commander Croft stated. "Every ship, every route, every departure time for the next two months. Everything the German wolf packs need to create a slaughter in the North Atlantic."

"But, sir!" Riley protested. "That's suicide! If they believe it, they'll sink our entire supply line!"

"They'll believe it," the commander said with grim certainty. "And that's the point. Every single piece of information in that message is false. A complete fabrication. While their U-boats are chasing phantom convoys in the middle of nowhere, the real convoys will be sailing a hundred miles south, completely unopposed. It could shorten the war by six months."

A heavy silence fell over the three men. The sheer audacity of the plan was staggering. To risk so much on a single, calculated lie.

"So our job was just to be the delivery boys," Riley said finally, a new respect for the quiet commander growing within him. "To get the bait into the water."

"Exactly," Croft agreed. "But there's always the unpredictable element. The little twist you can't account for. That's why we are here, in this submarine, running silent off the coast. If the Abwehr suspects a trick, if they break the code too fast and realize it's a plant, what do you think their first move will be?"

Neither of the young men answered. They didn't have to.

"They'll hunt the source," Croft finished for them. "They'll know a submarine delivered that device. They'll throw every destroyer and patrol boat they have into finding us, to make sure no more false information gets spread."

"So we're the backup," Riley murmured. "The lightning rod."

"You could put it that way," the commander nodded. "We sit here and wait. If we make it back to Scotland without incident, we know the bait has been taken. If we don't..."

He let the sentence hang in the pressurized air. He didn't need to finish it. The stakes were as clear as the cold sweat on Riley's brow.

"Well," Riley said, forcing a grin, "I've always said I'd rather be the lightning rod than the..."

He never finished his sentence, because at that moment a sharp, metallic ping echoed through the hull. Finch, who had been listening intently with his headphones, ripped them off his head.

"Sir!" he yelled, his face white as a sheet. "Active sonar! A destroyer, bearing zero-nine-zero, and it's close! It's hunting!"

spoke through the intercom, his voice a sharp, urgent crackle that sliced through the cabin's drone.
"Colonel Welsh, sir! We've got company!"
Colonel Welsh stiffened, his head snapping up. The brief smile he had worn moments before was gone, replaced by a mask of cold readiness. "What kind of company, Lieutenant?"
"Bandits, sir! Three of them, coming in fast at three o'clock high! Look like Ju-88s, heavily armed!"
Dawson and Farmer exchanged a look that was equal parts shock and grim understanding. The colonel's terrible hypothesis was no longer a theory. It was a deadly reality, streaking toward them through the black Atlantic sky.
"So," Welsh said, his voice dangerously quiet as he gripped the edge of the table. "They took the bait."
The B-25 suddenly lurched hard to port, throwing Dawson against the bulkhead. The deep hum of the engines rose to a screaming roar as the pilot began evasive maneuvers. Through the compartment window, the blackness was suddenly ripped apart by long, fiery streaks of light. The staccato hammering of the bomber's own .50 caliber machine guns joined the terrible symphony.
"They've opened up on us!" Dawson yelled over the din. He scrambled to the window, his pilot's instincts overriding everything else. He could just make out the sleek, twin-engined silhouettes of the German planes as they circled like sharks. "They're trying to box us in!"
"They aren't trying to shoot us down, not right away," Freddy Farmer observed, his voice steady despite the chaos. He was also pressed against the glass, his eyes narrowed in concentration. "Look at their approach. They're trying to force us down, to make us ditch in the water. They want the plane, and its passengers, intact if possible."
"The President," Welsh breathed, his face a pale stone in the dim light. "They think they can capture the President of the United States."
The horrible thought hung in the air, more terrifying than any cannon shell. The plane shuddered again as another burst of fire raked its tail. The top turret gunner was firing in long, desperate bursts, his tracers reaching out like fingers into the night, only to fall short.
"They're staying out of our effective range!" Dawson shouted in frustration. "Picking us apart from a distance!"
He felt like a caged animal. Here he was, an ace with dozens of aerial victories to his name, stuck in a passenger compartment while his countrymen fought for their lives just a few feet away. His hands clenched and unclenched. He had to do something.
"Colonel," he said, turning from the window. "With your permission, sir, Farmer and I are pilots. We might be able to help."
"Stay where you are, Dawson," Welsh ordered, though his eyes were fixed on the deadly dance outside. "You are passengers on this flight. The crew knows their job."
"But sir," Freddy protested, "we've fought these fellows before! We know their tricks!"
Before the colonel could reply, the intercom crackled again, this time with a cry of pain. "Copilot's hit! I'm hit! Medical kit, quick!"
That was all Dawson needed to hear. Rules and regulations vanished in the face of emergency. "That's it, sir, I'm going," he declared, already moving toward the narrow passage that led to the cockpit.
"Dawson, that's an order!" Welsh snapped.
"Sorry, sir!" Dawson called back over his shoulder. "You're the Chief of Intelligence, but right now that cockpit needs a pilot more than it needs a passenger!"
Freddy was right behind him. "What he said, sir!"
Colonel Welsh watched them go, a muscle twitching in his jaw. He made no move to stop them. He knew Dawson was right. The little item of fate he had spoken of had arrived, and it wore the black cross of the Luftwaffe.
Dawson squeezed his way forward, the plane bucking like a wild horse. He reached the cockpit to a scene of controlled chaos. The pilot, a young lieutenant with sweat pouring down his face, was wrestling with the controls. His left sleeve was soaked in blood. In the copilot's seat, a man slumped forward, unconscious, a dark stain spreading across his chest.
"Get him out of there!" Dawson yelled at Freddy, pointing to the wounded copilot. "I'll take his seat!"
The pilot glanced over, his eyes wide with surprise and pain. "Who the hell are you?"
"Dave Dawson! This is Freddy Farmer! Colonel Welsh sent us!" Dawson yelled, which was only partly a lie. "We're taking over!"
The pilot didn't argue. He was losing blood and the airplane was seconds from being shot out of the sky. With Freddy's help, they unstrapped the wounded copilot and carefully dragged him out of the seat and into the narrow space behind. Freddy immediately began tearing open a first-aid kit.
Dawson slid into the copilot's seat, his hands finding the controls as if by second nature. The familiar feel of the yoke in his grasp sent a surge of confidence through him. He was no longer a helpless passenger. He was home.
"What's our status?" he clipped, his eyes scanning the instrument panel.
"Left engine's sputtering, sir!" the pilot grunted, wincing in pain. "Took some shrapnel. Tail controls are sluggish. They shot up our hydraulics."
"Okay," Dawson said, his mind racing. "We're not going to outrun them, and we can't outclimb them. We have to fight them." He looked over at the pilot. "Can you still fly?"
"Yes, sir," the man said through gritted teeth. "Just tell me what to do."
"Good man," Dawson said. "What's your name?"
"Hanson, sir. Lieutenant Hanson."
"Alright, Hanson. On my mark, I want you to kick full right rudder and throw us into a slip. We'll present a bigger target for a second, but it will throw off their aim and maybe, just maybe, give our gunners a clearer shot. You ready?"
"Ready, sir!"
"Freddy!" Dawson yelled back. "How are you with a .50 caliber?"
"A bit out of practice, but willing to learn!" came the cheerful reply from the back. Freddy had finished patching up the copilot and was already crawling toward the waist gun position.
"Good! Get ready to give them a hot welcome!" Dawson looked out the windscreen. One of the Ju-88s was beginning its attack run. "Okay, Hanson... get ready... NOW!"
Hanson jammed his foot on the rudder pedal. The B-25 slid sideways in the air with a sickening lurch. For a heart-stopping moment, the bomber seemed to hang in the air, a perfect, unmissable target. The German pilot, caught by surprise at the unorthodox maneuver, corrected his aim, but it was too late. His stream of cannon fire passed just under their fuselage.
At the same time, the sideways motion gave the American gunners a new angle. The top turret, the belly turret, and Freddy's waist gun all opened up at once, converging their fire on the attacking Ju-88.
Dawson saw a beautiful and terrible sight. His tracers, and the tracers from the other guns, walked right up the German plane's fuselage and into its right engine. A bright orange flower of flame blossomed against the night. The Ju-88 faltered, then began to spiral down toward the dark, churning water below, a funeral pyre marking its grave.
"One down!" Hanson yelled, a triumphant grin briefly replacing his pained expression.
"Don't celebrate yet!" Dawson snapped, his eyes already on the other two attackers. "They'll be angry now! They're coming in from both sides!"
He was right. The remaining two German pilots, their hopes of capturing the plane dashed, were now committed to its destruction. They broke off in opposite directions, preparing to rake the B-25 in a coordinated crossfire.
"This is going to be rough," Dawson muttered. "Hanson, give me a shallow dive. We'll pick up speed. I want to try and drag them down low, to the deck. It'll mess with their attack angles."
The bomber nosed down, the scream of the wind rising. The two Ju-88s followed, their guns spitting fire. The cabin was filled with the deafening clang of cannon shells striking the fuselage. A hole the size of a man's fist appeared in the windscreen, showering the cockpit with plexiglass shards but miraculously missing both pilots.
"They're tearing us apart!" Hanson shouted.
"Just hold on!" Dawson urged. He watched one of the attackers, waiting for his moment. "Freddy, you see the one on the left?"
"I see him!" Freddy's voice crackled over the intercom, which he had managed to plug his headset into. "He's a bit shy, isn't he? Staying just out of reach!"
"I'm going to bring him closer!" Dawson said. He spoke to Hanson. "I'm taking the controls. When I bank, be ready to level us out."
Dawson hauled the yoke to the left, pulling the big bomber into a tight, shuddering turn, directly into the path of the oncoming fighter. It was a game of chicken, played at three hundred miles an hour, a thousand feet above the unforgiving ocean. For a second, it looked as though they would collide head-on. The German pilot, not expecting such an aggressive move from a lumbering bomber, flinched first. He banked sharply to avoid the collision, inadvertently exposing his plane's belly to the American gunners.
"NOW, FREDDY!" Dawson roared.
Freddy's gun, along with the belly turret, opened up in a furious, sustained burst. Tracers hammered into the soft underside of the Ju-88. The German plane seemed to stop in mid-air, then its entire wing section erupted in a massive fireball. The explosion lit up the night, momentarily turning the sea from black to a ghastly, shimmering orange.
"Two down!" Hanson gasped, his voice full of awe.
But their victory was short-lived. A sudden, violent jolt rocked the B-25, followed by the terrifying sound of shredding metal. The left engine, which had been sputtering, finally died with a cough and a plume of black smoke. The plane immediately began to yaw to the left, its one good engine trying to tear it apart.
"We've lost the port engine!" Hanson yelled, fighting the rudder pedals. "I can't hold her straight!"
"I've got it!" Dawson said, adding his own strength to the rudder, his leg muscles straining. They were losing altitude fast. Below them, the last Ju-88 was circling, coming up from behind for the killing blow.
"Colonel," Dawson said into the intercom, his voice strained. "We're in a bad way. One engine out, hydraulics shot. One bandit left, and he's on our tail."
Colonel Welsh's voice came back, impossibly calm. "I am aware of that, Dawson. Do what you have to do."
Dawson looked at the airspeed indicator. They were dropping like a stone. "We can't fight him, and we can't outrun him," he said, more to himself than to anyone else. Then an idea, a desperate, crazy idea, sparked in his mind.
"Freddy," he said. "How much ammunition do you have left?"
"Not much! Maybe one good burst!"
"Make it count!" Dawson ordered. "Hanson, when I give the word, I want you to cut the power to the good engine. Just for a second."
"Cut the power?" Hanson said, looking at him as if he were insane. "Sir, we'll stall! We'll fall right out of the sky!"
"That's what I'm counting on!" Dawson said, a grim smile on his face. "The German pilot thinks we're crippled and running. He's going to get cocky. He's going to fly right up our tailpipe for an easy kill. When he does, we're going to slam on the brakes."
It was a maneuver that should have been impossible, a fighter pilot's trick in a heavy bomber. But it was all they had left.
"He's closing!" the tail gunner's voice crackled. "Five hundred yards! Four hundred!"
Dawson could almost feel the German pilot's eyes on the back of his neck. He watched the dark waves rushing up to meet them.
"Three hundred yards!"
"Get ready, Hanson..." Dawson breathed.
"He's opening fire!"
Tracers streamed past the cockpit.
"NOW, HANSON! CUT IT!"
Hanson yanked the throttle lever back. The B-25's one good engine fell silent. The effect was instantaneous and dramatic. The bomber, suddenly robbed of all forward thrust, seemed to stop in the air. It shuddered, stalled, and began to drop like an elevator with a snapped cable.
The German pilot, speeding in for the kill, was completely unprepared. He saw his target suddenly brake in front of him. With no time to react, he overshot them, flying directly over the top of the B-25.
For a single, beautiful second, the Ju-88 filled the sights of every gun on the American bomber's top side.
"FIRE!" Dawson screamed.
Every gun that could still bear opened up. Freddy, the top turret gunner, even Hanson with the fixed nose guns, all fired at once. They couldn't miss. Their combined fire tore into the German plane at point blank range. The Ju-88 disintegrated in a flash of light and a cloud of debris that rained down on the falling B-25.
"Power, Hanson! Full power!" Dawson yelled.
Hanson slammed the throttle forward. The right engine coughed, sputtered, then caught with a thunderous roar. Dawson fought the controls, pulling the nose up just as the bomber's belly threatened to kiss the tops of the waves. The B-25 staggered, groaned, but slowly, agonizingly, it began to climb again, away from the hungry sea.
Silence descended on the cockpit, broken only by the drone of the single engine and the whistling of the wind through the new holes in the fuselage.
After a long moment, Freddy's voice came over the intercom, shaky but alive. "Well," he said. "That was a bit of a sticky wicket, wasn't it?"
Dawson let out a breath he didn't know he'd been holding and leaned back in his seat, his arms aching. He looked over at Hanson. The young pilot was pale and bleeding, but he was grinning from ear to ear.
"You were right, sir," Hanson said. "You slammed on the brakes."
Dawson managed a weak grin in return. "Just an old trick."
He looked out at the vast, empty darkness. There were no more bandits. They had survived. But the cost had been high. The B-25 was a wreck, flying on one engine and a prayer.
Colonel Welsh appeared at the cockpit door, his face grim but his eyes shining with a fierce light. He looked at the dead engine, the shattered instruments, the holes in the windscreen.
"Report," he said, his voice all business.
"Three bandits down, sir," Dawson replied, his voice tired. "But we're badly damaged. We've lost the port engine. Hydraulics are gone. We're losing fuel from a dozen leaks. The wounded are stable, for now." He paused, then asked the question that was on everyone's mind. "Can we make it to Casablanca, sir?"
Colonel Welsh stared out at the smoking engine for a long moment, the single functioning propeller beating a desperate rhythm against the night.
"No, Dawson," he said slowly, turning back to them. "There's no way we can reach Casablanca now. Not even close."
He let the weight of that statement settle over the exhausted crew. The elation of their victory evaporated, replaced by the cold, hard reality of their situation. They were hundreds of miles from land, in a crippled airplane, with dawn still hours away.
"Then what do we do, sir?" Hanson asked, his voice small.
Colonel Welsh's eyes moved from Dawson to Farmer, who had joined him at the door, and then to Hanson. He had his answer. The enemy knew. The enemy had tried to intercept the President's supposed plane. The first, most dangerous part of his intelligence test was complete. The result was a resounding, terrifying success.
"We change the plan," the colonel said, his voice taking on a new hardness. "We have proven that the route is compromised. Now, we have a new objective."
"Which is what, sir?" Dawson asked.
"To survive," Colonel Welsh stated simply. "We find the nearest strip of land, no matter how small or insignificant, and we put this airplane down before it falls into the sea. Then, our journey really begins."

The lens of a binocular.

They were being watched.

"This is our chance," the colonel whispered. "They've split up. Dawson, you and I will take the two heading for the fire. Farmer, you will deal with the two on the beach. Peeking through the leaves, Dawson saw the German officer and his companion stop about thirty yards from the fire. The officer was talking, pointing at the sand. He'd found their tracks leading from the water. Colonel Welsh touched Dawson's arm and pointed. He would take the officer. Dawson was to take the other man. He held up three fingers, then slowly folded them down. Three. Two. One. On zero, they would move. Dawson's breath caught in his throat. Dawson was a half second behind him. The sailor he was targeting must have sensed something at the last moment, for he started to turn. It was too late. Dawson crashed into him, one hand clamping over the man's mouth, the other driving the butt of his pistol hard into the base of his skull. The man went limp without a sound. He moved swiftly back to their observation post. Dawson followed, his senses on high alert. Peering through the leaves, they saw a single figure dragging two bodies from the water's edge into the shadows of the rocks. It was Freddy. He had done his job. The beach was empty. The raft sat by the water. Out at sea, the U-boat waited patiently. "Good lad," the colonel muttered with a flicker of approval. He raised his hand and gave a short, sharp whistle. A moment later, Freddy appeared at their side, his breathing heavy. "Two down, sir," he reported, wiping his knife clean on a leaf. "No trouble." "Well done, Farmer," Welsh said. He then turned his gaze back to the U-boat. "Now for the interesting part. They're expecting a signal. We're going to give them one." He looked at Dawson. "You're a pilot, Dawson. You know signals. It was a simple device, with a shutter operated by a small key. "They'll have a code," Dawson said. "'All clear,' or 'danger,' or 'found survivors.'" "Of course they will," the colonel said. "And we don't know it. So we can't send 'all clear.' But we can send something else. Something that will bring them in." He stared at the U-boat, his mind clearly working at lightning speed. "They know a plane has crashed. They've sent a scouting party. The party does not return or signal. What would you do if you were that U-boat commander?" "I'd be suspicious," Freddy offered. "I might send another party. Or shell the beach." "Or," the colonel said, a thin, wolfish smile touching his lips, "if you received a signal that said 'Found survivors. High value target confirmed. "You'd bring your boat in as close as you could, and you'd land a larger, heavily armed force to capture the prize. You wouldn't risk shelling the beach and killing a 'high value target.' You'd want him alive." "But sir, we don't know the code for that message!" Dawson protested. "We don't need to," the colonel replied, holding up the lamp. "Urgency is a universal language. "We don't need their codes," the colonel said, his eyes glittering with a hard, dangerous light. "We are going to use their radio." He gestured toward the U-boat. "Every one of these subs has a radio. And that officer," he pointed to the body of the German leader, "will have the frequency and the call signs for his boat. Dawson stared at him, dumbfounded. "Sir? You want us to get on their radio frequency and--and what? Pretend to be them?"

"Not exactly," Colonel Welsh said. "Think it through. A German shore party lands. A firefight ensues. Then, silence. Sometime later, a new voice comes on the radio. An American voice. He reports, in clear English, that the German landing party has been eliminated, and that President Roosevelt and his staff are now secure. He can issue a warning for the U-boat to stand off or be destroyed."

"But--but they'll know it's a trick!" Dawson protested. "We don't have a way to destroy a submarine!"

"Of course they'll know that part's a bluff," the colonel agreed patiently. "But the rest of it? An American voice, claiming to have the President? The U-boat commander will hear it. A message, supposedly from the enemy, on their own tactical frequency, claiming to have captured the American President on a deserted island after a firefight with one of their own U-boats. It's confusing. It's unbelievable. And because it's so unbelievable, parts of it might just seem true."

He let the idea hang there. "It will sow confusion. It will delay any decision to shell this beach. And while they are confused, while they are trying to figure out what in blazes is going on, we will be carrying out the _real_ plan."

"And what's that, sir?" Dawson asked, feeling as though he were perpetually one step behind the colonel's racing mind.

Colonel Welsh looked from Dawson to Freddy, and then back to the captured German raft sitting by the water's edge.

"That U-boat commander," he said quietly, "is expecting us to stay here. He thinks we are trapped. He thinks he has us pinned down. He would never, in a million years, expect us to do the one thing that is tactically insane." He pointed a finger at the raft. "He would never expect us to come to him."

Dawson gritted his teeth against the pain and dug his paddle into the water. Behind them, the U-boat was a scene of chaos. Lights flickered and died. More smoke poured from the hatch. Colonel Welsh was already on his feet, his face a granite mask as he braced himself against the bulkhead. "Dawson! Farmer! Get to the waist guns! The gunners are--"

He and Freddy lunged for the waist gun positions. The regular gunners were slumped over in their harnesses, their bodies still. There was no time for grief, no time for anything but action. Dawson grabbed the handles of the .50 caliber machine gun on the starboard side, the cold metal a familiar, grim comfort in his hands. Freddy took the port side gun.
Through the plexiglass bubble, Dawson saw them. Two sleek, shark-like Messerschmitt 109s, their yellow noses glinting in the moonlight. They were peeling off for another pass.
"Here they come!" Freddy yelled, his voice tight but steady.
Dawson swung the heavy gun, lining up the glowing tracer sight on the lead fighter as it banked in. The German pilot was good, coming in from below where the bomber's profile was largest. Dawson held his fire, his knuckles white. He waited, letting the fighter grow larger and larger in his sights, a deadly game of chicken played out at three hundred miles an hour, twenty thousand feet above the dark Atlantic.
"Now!" he roared to himself, and squeezed the trigger.
The B-25 bucked and vibrated as the big machine gun hammered out its song of death. A stream of tracers reached out, a glowing red finger pointing across the night sky. He saw them stitch a line across the Messerschmitt's wing root. A puff of black smoke, then a glorious, brilliant orange blossom of flame. The German fighter faltered, its nose dipped, and it began a long, fiery spiral toward the sea below.
"Got him!" Dawson yelled, a savage cry of triumph. "One down!"
"Watch it!" Freddy shouted from the other side. "The other one is coming around!"
The second fighter had learned from his comrade's mistake. Instead of a straight pass, he came in a twisting, corkscrew approach, spitting cannon fire that ripped more holes in their already battered plane. The lights in the cabin flickered and died, plunging them into near total darkness, lit only by the muzzle flashes of the guns and the moonlit clouds outside.
"I can't get a bead on him!" Freddy cursed. "He's all over the place!"
Colonel Welsh was at Dawson's side, his hand on Dawson's shoulder. "Their base must be on the coast of French West Africa," the colonel shouted over the din. "They were waiting for us! My decoy plan worked too well! They think we're the prize!"
The irony was so bitter it almost made Dawson laugh. They had set themselves up as bait, and the sharks were now tearing them apart.
The B-25's pilot was fighting the controls, trying to evade, but the bomber was a lumbering beast compared to the nimble fighter. Another burst of fire raked them, and this time Dawson felt a sharp, stinging pain in his side as a piece of shrapnel from the exploding bulkhead tore through his flight suit. He grunted but kept his eyes glued to the sky.
"He's coming in for the kill!" the colonel yelled. "He's going for the cockpit!"
Dawson saw it too. The German plane was leveling off for a head-on pass, a suicidal maneuver designed to take out the pilots and send the bomber plunging out of control. Their own pilot banked the B-25 sharply, a desperate move that sent everything not tied down crashing against the walls. The maneuver exposed their belly.
"Freddy! Now's your chance!" Dawson screamed.
Through his own window, he saw the Messerschmitt flash underneath them, its canopy just yards away. He saw Freddy's gun swivel down, and then the night was ripped apart by the roar of Freddy's .50 caliber. The tracers vanished into the German fighter's belly and cockpit. For a heart-stopping second, the two planes flew locked together, one hunter, one prey. Then the Messerschmitt's engine exploded in a shower of sparks and metal. The plane cartwheeled away into the darkness, a broken, burning wreck.
Silence fell, a heavy, ringing silence broken only by the whistle of the wind through the new holes in their plane and the sputtering cough of the port engine.
"Damage report!" the pilot's voice crackled, strained and tense. "What's our status back there?"
Colonel Welsh picked up a handset. "Welsh here. Both bandits destroyed. We have casualties in the gunnery compartment. Dawson is wounded, but it doesn't look serious. How are we doing up there?"
"Port engine is shot to pieces," the pilot's voice came back, grim. "We're losing fuel and altitude. There's no way we're making Casablanca, Colonel. We'll be lucky to make the coast."
"Understood," Colonel Welsh said, his voice as calm as if he were ordering breakfast. "Do the best you can. We'll ride it down with you."
He turned to Dawson. "Let me see that," he said, pointing to Dawson's side.
Dawson looked down. His flight suit was dark with blood, but the pain had subsided into a dull throb. "It's just a scratch, sir," he said, though his head was starting to feel light.
"So was the last one," Freddy said, coming over to help. His face was smudged with cordite, but his eyes were shining with the fierce light of battle. "You've got to stop collecting these souvenirs, Yank."

"I don't feel very lucky, sir," Dawson mumbled, the adrenaline finally wearing off and leaving a deep, aching exhaustion in its place.
"We're alive," the colonel stated simply. "The enemy is at the bottom of the ocean. The information they thought they had is wrong. And they've lost three aircraft and a U-boat trying to act on it. From an intelligence standpoint, this is a resounding success."
"Remind me never to volunteer for one of your successes again, sir," Dawson said with a weak grin.
Freddy chuckled. "Hear, hear."
The pilot's voice crackled over the intercom again, pulling them all back to their immediate problem. "Land in sight! It looks like a beach. I'm going to try and put her down on the sand. Brace for impact!"
Colonel Welsh helped Dawson to a seat and strapped him in tightly. "Hold on, son," he said, his hand gripping Dawson's shoulder. "This is going to be rough."
Dawson looked out the window. In the pale light of the moon, he could see a long, white strip of sand bordering a dark, dense jungle. And beyond that, the dark, churning Atlantic. The pilot was bringing them in low over the waves, the one good engine roaring in protest. The landing gear was down. It was a desperate gamble. If the sand was too soft, they'd flip over. If the gear collapsed, the plane would cartwheel and break apart.
"Here we go!" the pilot yelled.
The plane touched down. For a moment, there was a smooth, gliding sensation. Then the wheels dug into the soft sand, and the world dissolved into a nightmare of sound and violence. The B-25 slewed sideways, its tires screaming, its landing gear groaning under the immense strain. Metal shrieked as the port propeller, its engine dead, dug a deep furrow in the beach. The plane spun around, a great wounded bird, before the landing gear finally gave way with a sickening crunch. The bomber collapsed onto its belly, sliding for another hundred yards in a shower of sand and sparks before finally, blessedly, coming to a halt.
The silence that followed was more profound than any that had come before. It was the silence of survival.
"Is everyone all right?" Colonel Welsh's voice cut through the haze.
A chorus of groans and "ayes" came from the cockpit and the rest of the crew who had survived. Dawson unstrapped himself, his body aching from a dozen new bruises. He, Freddy, and the Colonel, along with the two pilots, were the only ones left. They had made it. They were alive, stranded on a deserted beach somewhere on the coast of Africa, with a wrecked plane and a world of trouble ahead of them.
"Well, Colonel," Dawson said, his voice hoarse, as they all stood on the sand looking at the broken bomber silhouetted against the rising sun. "What's the plan now?"
Colonel Welsh stared at the jungle that bordered the beach, his expression unreadable. "First, we destroy the sensitive equipment and codes. Then, we assess our position. And then," he said, turning to look at them, a familiar hard glint in his eyes, "we find a way to finish our mission. The President's safety still depends on us getting those new orders to Natal."
"But our plane is a wreck, sir," the pilot, a young captain named Miller, pointed out. "And we're a thousand miles from anywhere."
"Details, Captain, details," the colonel said, and for the first time since they had been attacked, he allowed himself a small, thin smile. "In my line of work, you learn one thing very quickly. The mission is never over until you say it is."
Dawson looked from the wrecked plane to the impenetrable jungle, then back to the determined face of his commanding officer. He didn't know how, but he had a strange feeling that Colonel Welsh was right. This crazy, deadly, world-shaking adventure was far from over. It was just getting started. All over again.
